Wars Across The World is a deeply traditional, methodical strategy title that deliberately embraces the logic and pacing of classic tabletop wargames rather than the spectacle of modern real-time strategy. Developed by Strategiae and published by Plug In Digital alongside Avalon Digital, it presents itself as a grand historical sandbox where conflicts from vastly different eras are modeled using a single, consistent rule set. From ancient wars to twentieth-century global conflicts, the game’s ambition lies not in cinematic flair but in offering a broad, intellectually demanding overview of warfare across time.

The game is built around standalone scenarios rather than a continuous campaign, and this structure defines much of its appeal. Each scenario represents a specific historical conflict, complete with asymmetrical forces, political constraints, and geographically defined objectives. Players are free to jump between eras without needing to relearn the core mechanics, which creates a strong sense of continuity despite the massive historical range. Once the fundamentals of movement, combat resolution, command structure, and event cards are understood, they apply just as readily to ancient battles as they do to modern ones, reinforcing the idea that the game is about strategic principles rather than technological detail.

Gameplay operates at an operational level, with armies and formations moving between large regions instead of individual hexes or tiles. This abstraction keeps the focus on high-level decision-making such as where to commit forces, when to press an offensive, and how to maintain momentum while protecting supply and cohesion. Leaders play a critical role, influencing combat effectiveness, morale, and movement, while event cards introduce uncertainty through historical twists like weather shifts, reinforcements, political changes, or logistical complications. These systems combine to create a steady rhythm of planning, execution, and adaptation that rewards foresight over impulse.

The pace of Wars Across The World is deliberately slow and contemplative. Turns often involve careful evaluation of the map, weighing long-term consequences rather than reacting to immediate threats. This can feel deeply satisfying for players who enjoy deliberate planning and historical what-if scenarios, but it can also feel dry or overwhelming for those accustomed to faster or more visually dynamic strategy games. The game expects patience and attention, and it does little to soften its learning curve beyond basic tutorials, effectively assuming that its audience is already comfortable with traditional wargame concepts.

Visually, the presentation is utilitarian and firmly rooted in board-game sensibilities. Maps are clean and readable, with a focus on clarity over decoration. Unit counters, control markers, and terrain features are designed to communicate information efficiently rather than impress aesthetically. While this approach serves gameplay well during long sessions, it may come across as dated or austere to players expecting detailed unit models or cinematic effects. The interface follows the same philosophy, prioritizing function and density of information over accessibility or modern UI polish.

Artificial intelligence remains one of the more debated aspects of the experience. In some scenarios, the AI provides a solid and credible opponent that forces careful planning and punishes overextension. In others, it can behave passively or make questionable strategic choices, occasionally undermining the tension of a solo match. As a result, the game often shines brightest when approached as a historical simulation or puzzle rather than a consistently challenging competitive experience. For dedicated players, much of the enjoyment comes from exploring scenarios, testing alternative strategies, and understanding how small decisions can cascade into large historical shifts.

Content breadth is both a strength and a point of contention. The base game offers a meaningful selection of scenarios, but a significant portion of the total content is distributed through additional downloadable scenarios. These expansions greatly increase the game’s scope and replay value, but they also fragment the experience, making the full package feel more like a long-term investment than a single, complete product. Players who enjoy the core mechanics will find plenty of reasons to expand their library, while newcomers may prefer to approach cautiously and selectively.

In the end, Wars Across The World is a niche but sincere tribute to historical wargaming traditions. It favors depth, abstraction, and historical breadth over accessibility or spectacle, offering a strategic playground that spans centuries with remarkable consistency. For players who appreciate thoughtful, turn-based warfare and are willing to engage with a demanding ruleset, it provides a rich and intellectually rewarding experience. Those seeking streamlined mechanics or modern presentation may struggle with its rigidity, but for its intended audience, it stands as a quietly ambitious and enduring strategy title.

------------------------------------------------

The concept is *fantastic*: learn one board wargame rules set and be able to play operational/strategic campaigns from literally *any* historical era.**

That said, that rules set is a snarling b!tch to learn (and this from a half-century veteran of tabletop and computer wargames). The in-game tutorial shows little more than how to move units. To learn the game you'll need to suffer through a long, badly-proofread translated manual which reads like neither the original writer nor the translator were proficient in *either* language. BUT...

Once you've read the manual and played a couple of games to get a handle on the rules mechanics and the sequence of play, you're in for a treat. It's true that no two plays of a scenario will ever be the same, not just because of each player's card deck and dice-driven combat, but because the A.I. reacts differently from game to game. I've played the Caesar 58BC scenario (in which the AI moves first) about ten times now, and I've seen the AI execute at least three different Turn One-Two plans  (presumably because of different card draws each time).

Bear in mind, this is no "The Operational Art of War". The complexity here is about a 4 on the standard wargame 1-10 scale. It's made a bit difficult to learn because of the manual's presentation, not because it's an inherently difficult game. And if you wait for the half-price sales to buy Season Packs of scenarios, you can enjoy a LOT of different wargames for the price of a single GMT/Compass tabletop game -- and not have to learn a brand-new set of rules each time.

**This was a sort of "grail quest" for tabletop wargame companies back in the day (SPI's "Strategy I"/Yaquinto's "Battle: The Game of Strategy"). These failed to deliver primarily because they *were* generic; different periods lacked period flavor. Wars Across the World avoids this trap by a) using different graphics for different periods and b) devising scenario-specific rules to better represent the challenges of the campaign in question.

[h1]Turn-based game with gameplay modifiers, dice rolls, unit cards, and hit counters.[/h1]

The core gameplay is basically a board game with unit cards with hit counters, dice rolls, and cards you can play to affect gameplay in various ways (introduce new units to the board, get bonuses during battle, increase income, etc.) It's basically a deeper and more historical alternative to Risk.

[h1]Potentially awesome game held back by some weirdly impenetrable UI[/h1]

I really like the range of scenarios and core gameplay for this game. However, after playing it for 10 hours and doing the tutorial twice, I still haven't figured out how to move air units (whenever I move them they just turn up back at the old airbase again) so I literally have air units that can't participate in battle...

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2736856992

(UPDATE: The way to reposition air units is to move them to a city with an airbase but you have to mouse over the CITY and not the TERRITORY.)

Other aspects of the game can be incredibly impenetrable as well such as this screen which literally prevented me from finishing the game until I complained about it and eventually figured out after getting a response that you have to select units (which actually gives them hits rather than killing them) until the red number is zero in each column.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2735246594

This game needs a more complete tutorial and some improvements to the UI.

[h1]Huge range of (mostly DLC) scenarios[/h1]

Because this is basically a board game, it is able to cover wars ranging from the classical era to the 21st century. Most of it is DLC and buying all the DLC will get fairly pricey.

[h1]P.S.[/h1]

I DID enjoy this game more than [i]Drive on Moscow[/i] which I couldn't stick with long enough to review.

The game looks and plays like a classic boardgame, with different phases going step by step. I like turn-based wargames as they leave time to think about the next moves, and also because I could adapt the pace to my preferences of the moment (personally I like to take it slow after a day at work, and turn-based games are great to relax).

The system is simple and elegant, and whoever has some experience on boardgaming/wargaming should be able to get it in a flash. The manual is exhaustive, so in case of doubts is possible to go with the old-fashioned way and read it to get into the finer details of the system.

Frankly I had some difficulty learning the game.  I sat down with some spare time to read the War Across the World game manual. I did this after having challenges posed by the quick start info that didn't have critical information and the challenges posed by the Tutorial, nothing seemed to work properly. Having read the 100+ page manual (which has a lot of repeated information, sometimes with added content that wasn't mentioned earlier) I figured the game out and was able to play as I think it was intended.  I was frustrated by the challenge. For me it was the organization of critical gameplay info and the rules being the second language of the writers took a lot for me to overcome. I first completed Missouri 1861. A small interesting and compact scenario that I was able to replay quickly and put it all together. It wasn't as difficult to play compared to some - no airpower or naval forces to deal with.  Subsequently, I played Berlin 1945, Manassas 1861 and Waterloo 1815 and enjoyed them. Currently I am working on the Premium Spain 1936 DLC. I feel that the larger scenarios may have greater staying power than the more compact ones based on my experience thus far. Spain is a wonderfully large and complicated scenario with what I think may be worth repeated play.  I will continue to work my way through the scenarios that come with the game and buy those other DLC that interest me.

Great series of not too complicated war games on a variety of interesting and unusual topics  - most can be played in two hours and give useful historical insights into the conflicts they portray.  In my mind,  these are the spiritual successor to the SPI Strategy and Tactics magazine games of the 1970's, which provided provided a unique window into interesting and/or unfamiliar historical events at a reasonable price point.
I gotta say i'm a fan. I suggest a Soviet-Afghan War module.

Unfortunately, I can no longer recommend this game.  The last update was Sept 2022, two and a half years ago.  For all intents and purposes, WAW is dead and abandoned.

I can certainly recommend SGS (Strategy Game Studio) games as they are running on the same engine, but SGS is very active, prices are reasonable, and the engine is constantly being updated and expanded.

While SGS does not have the large number of DLC that  WAW has, what they do have is varied and is also being expanded.  Their offerings are full games though, not DLC like WAW.

I was very sorry to see WAW wither and die.  I felt it had a lot of potential going forward.
